lesson_scope: Rings and beads threaded on rough vertical and horizontal rods; normal contact force provided by horizontal components; dual limiting equilibrium thresholds (upward versus downward slipping); self-locking jamming conditions on vertical poles; zero normal reaction states and unresisted acceleration; and variable geometry pulley coupling.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 1: Minimum horizontal force to prevent ring slipping down vertical wire

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 1: Minimum horizontal force to prevent ring slipping down vertical wire

hints: On a vertical wire, the horizontal push provides the normal reaction: $R = P$.
To prevent the ring sliding down, upward limiting friction must balance weight: $\mu R = mg \implies 0.4P = 5 \implies P = 12.5\text{ N}$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify forces acting on the ring along horizontal and vertical axes:
- Horizontal balance: $R = P$.
- Vertical balance at the verge of sliding down:
$$\Sigma F_y = F - mg = 0 \implies F = mg = 0.5(10) = 5\text{ N}$$

Apply the limiting friction law $F = \mu R$:
$$0.4 P = 5 \implies P = \frac{5}{0.4} = 12.5\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Analyze the contact forces:
- The horizontal push presses the ring into the wire with reaction:
$$R = P$$
- Gravity pulls the ring downwards with weight:
$$W = mg = 0.5 \times 10 = 5\text{ N}$$

Find the holding push:
- Limiting friction acts upwards to prevent downward slip:
$$0.4P = 5 \implies P_{\min} = 12.5\text{ N}$$

ai_rubric.observable: Identifies that normal reaction is $R = P$ and that upward limiting friction balances weight: $\mu P = mg = 0.5(10) = 5\text{ N}$.
Solves $0.4P = 5$ to obtain $P_{\min} = 12.5\text{ N}$.

questions.difficulty_reason: Foundational Drill: Drill 3: Upward versus downward slip tendency on vertical rod

source_evidence.structural_inspiration: Drill 3: Upward versus downward slip tendency on vertical rod

hints: The upward pull ($11\text{ N}$) is greater than the downward weight ($6\text{ N}$), so the ring tends to slide upwards.
Friction opposes the tendency of motion, so it acts downwards. Form vertical equilibrium: $11 = 6 + F_f \implies F_f = 5\text{ N}$ downwards.

walkthrough.text:
Determine the net vertical tendency without friction:
- Upward pull: $11\text{ N}$.
- Downward weight: $mg = 0.6(10) = 6\text{ N}$.
Since $11\text{ N} > 6\text{ N}$, the ring tends to slide upwards, so friction must act downwards:
$$\Sigma F_y = 11 - 6 - F_f = 0$$

Calculate the actual friction force and check against the maximum threshold:
$$F_f = 11 - 6 = 5\text{ N} \quad (\text{downwards})$$
Note that $F_{\max} = \mu R = 0.5(14) = 7\text{ N}$. Since $5\text{ N} < 7\text{ N}$, the ring is safely held in static equilibrium:
$$F_f = 5\text{ N} < F_{\max}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Check which way the ring wants to move:
- Upward force is $11\text{ N}$, while weight is only $6\text{ N}$:
$$F_\text{pull, y} > W \implies 11\text{ N} > 6\text{ N}$$
The upward pull wins, meaning the ring tends to slide upwards.

Determine the opposing friction:
- Friction resists upward motion by pointing downwards:
$$F_f = 11 - 6 = 5\text{ N} \quad (\text{downwards})$$
Since maximum grip is $\mu R = 7\text{ N}$, static friction easily supplies the required $5\text{ N}$.

ai_rubric.observable: Compares upward pull ($11\text{ N}$) with downward weight ($6\text{ N}$) to deduce that the ring tends to move upwards.
Calculates friction force $F_f = 11 - 6 = 5\text{ N}$ acting downwards (noting $5\text{ N} < F_{\max} = 7\text{ N}$).

hints: Resolve horizontally perpendicular to the rod: the normal reaction is $R = T_1\cos 40^\circ$.

walkthrough.text:
Identify normal reaction and friction for upward slipping:
- Horizontal equilibrium perpendicular to the vertical rod:
$$\Sigma F_x = R - T_1\cos 40^\circ = 0 \implies R = T_1\cos 40^\circ$$
- Limiting friction opposes upward motion by acting downwards:
$$F = \mu R = 0.35 T_1\cos 40^\circ$$

Set up vertical equilibrium:
$$\Sigma F_y = T_1\sin 40^\circ - mg - F = 0$$
$$T_1\sin 40^\circ - 5 - 0.35 T_1\cos 40^\circ = 0$$
$$T_1(\sin 40^\circ - 0.35\cos 40^\circ) = 5$$

Evaluate the trigonometric coefficients and solve for $T_1$:
$$\sin 40^\circ - 0.35\cos 40^\circ \approx 0.642788 - 0.35(0.766044) = 0.642788 - 0.268115 = 0.374673$$
$$T_1 = \frac{5}{0.374673} \approx 13.345 \approx 13.3\text{ N}$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Find normal contact force:
- The horizontal pull presses the ring against the rod:
$$R = T_1\cos 40^\circ$$
- Downward resisting friction is $0.35 T_1\cos 40^\circ$.

Balance vertical forces:
- The upward pull $T_1\sin 40^\circ$ must overcome both weight and friction:
$$T_1\sin 40^\circ = 5 + 0.35 T_1\cos 40^\circ$$

Calculate the upward slip tension:
$$T_1(0.6428 - 0.2681) = 5 \implies T_1 \approx 13.3\text{ N}$$
A tension of $13.3\text{ N}$ pulls the ring upwards.

Apply horizontal balance to determine tension $T_B$:
Because the wire exerts no normal reaction ($R = 0$), the horizontal components of tension must be equal and opposite:
$$\Sigma F_x = T_B\cos 45^\circ - 20\cos 30^\circ = 0$$
$$T_B\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 20\left(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = 10\sqrt{3}$$
$$T_B = \frac{20\sqrt{3}}{\sqrt{2}} = 10\sqrt{6} \approx 24.4949 \approx 24.5\text{ N}$$

Compute vertical forces acting on the ring:
- Upward force from string $AR$:
$$F_\text{up} = 20\sin 30^\circ = 20(0.5) = 10\text{ N}$$
- Downward force from string $BR$:
$$F_{B,y} = T_B\sin 45^\circ = (10\sqrt{6})\left(\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2}\right) = 10\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3205\text{ N}$$
- Downward weight:
$$W = mg = 1.5(10) = 15\text{ N}$$

Determine the resultant downward vertical force:
$$F_\text{down, total} = 15 + 17.3205 = 32.3205\text{ N}$$
$$F_\text{net} = 32.3205 - 10 = 22.3205 \approx 22.3\text{ N} \quad (\text{downwards})$$

teacher_walkthrough.text:
Balance the horizontal tug-of-war:
- Zero reaction means horizontal pulls match:
$$T_B\cos 45^\circ = 20\cos 30^\circ \implies T_B = 10\sqrt{6} \approx 24.5\text{ N}$$

Sum downward loading:
- Weight is $15\text{ N}$ and downward pull is $17.32\text{ N}$:
$$F_\text{down} = 15 + 17.32 = 32.32\text{ N}$$

Find net vertical force:
- Subtract the $10\text{ N}$ upward pull:
$$F_\text{net} = 32.32 - 10 = 22.3\text{ N} \quad (\text{downwards})$$

Calculates net downward force: $15 + T_B\sin 45^\circ - 20\sin 30^\circ = 15 + 10\sqrt{3} - 10 \approx 22.3\text{ N}$.

hints: The normal reaction on the pole is the horizontal component of the pull: $R = P\cos 30^\circ$.

Factor out $P$: $P(\sin 30^\circ + 0.6\cos 30^\circ) = 20 \implies P(0.5 + 0.5196) = 20 \implies P \approx 19.6\text{ N}$.

Find normal reaction perpendicular to the vertical pole:
$$\Sigma F_x = R - P\cos 30^\circ = 0 \implies R = P\cos 30^\circ$$

$$\Sigma F_y = P\sin 30^\circ + \mu R - W = 0$$
$$P\sin 30^\circ + 0.6(P\cos 30^\circ) = 20$$

Evaluate the trigonometric coefficients:
$$P(0.5 + 0.6\cos 30^\circ) = 20$$
$$0.5 + 0.6(0.866025) = 0.5 + 0.519615 = 1.019615$$

$$P_{\min} = \frac{20}{1.019615} \approx 19.6153 \approx 19.6\text{ N}$$

$$P(0.5 + 0.6\cos 30^\circ) = 20\text{ N}$$

$$P(1.0196) = 20 \implies P_{\min} \approx 19.6\text{ N}$$

hints: To slip upwards, the upward pulling component $P\sin 30^\circ$ must overcome both weight ($20\text{ N}$) and downward limiting friction ($0.6 P\cos 30^\circ$).

Notice that $\sin 30^\circ - 0.6\cos 30^\circ = 0.5 - 0.5196 = -0.0196 < 0$, which means that increasing $P$ actually increases downward resistance faster than upward pull.

$$\sin 30^\circ - 0.6\cos 30^\circ = 0.5 - 0.519615 = -0.019615 < 0$$
Alternatively, observe that the angle of pull satisfies:
$$\tan 30^\circ = \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 0.57735 < \mu = 0.6$$
Because $\tan 30^\circ < \mu$, increasing the pulling force $P$ increases the normal reaction and resisting friction more rapidly than it increases the upward lifting component.

Conclude the jamming condition and complete equilibrium range:
Because $F_\text{net, up} < -20\text{ N} < 0$ for all $P > 0$, the ring can never slip upwards regardless of how large $P$ becomes (self-locking jamming condition). The complete range of values of $P$ for which the ring remains in equilibrium is:
$$P \geqslant 19.6\text{ N}$$

- Since $0.52 P > 0.5 P$, friction grows faster than the lift!

$$\tan 30^\circ < \mu \implies 0.577 < 0.6$$

State the equilibrium range:
- The ring never slips upwards, so equilibrium holds for all forces above threshold:
$$P \geqslant 19.6\text{ N}$$
